## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Two goals in this second part. We learn about three advanced object types —
factor, data.frame and tibble. And we understand how they relate to the basic
types we discussed in part one.

The second goal is the more important one: none of these three is genuinely new.
Each of them is one of the basic types with something added.

## Slide 4 · The picture, extended

Here is the hierarchy from part one, extended by the two types we deal with now.

Look at the dotted arrows, because they carry the whole message of this session.
A factor is not a new kind of thing — it is an integer vector with something
added. A data frame is not a new kind of thing either — it is a list with
something added.

If you hold on to that, both types stop being mysterious, and the functions you
already know keep working on them.

## Slide 5 · On more advanced object types

While there are many object types in R, understanding the basics is key. They
are by far the most common ones, and all other object types are somehow built
upon the basic types by adding attributes.

Among the special types, two stand out in their prevalence.

Factors, for categorical data: they can take one out of a pre-specified number of
values, called levels. The classical example is male, female, diverse. They are
created using the function `factor()`.

And data frames, in the two variants `data.frame` and `tibble`: a kind of table
in which different variables are stored as vectors. Tibbles are a modern variant
that, as the slogan goes, do less and complain more — which is a virtue, because
complaining early beats failing silently later.

Others that we will not cover here are, for example, matrices, durations or
dates.

## Slide 6 · Digression: attributes

To turn our basic object types into something more fancy we can give them
attributes, one of which is called class. This changes their behaviour when
functions are applied to them.

Technically, adding a class attribute changes the class but not the type. Run
the three lines: `typeof(ff)` returns integer, `class(ff)` returns factor, and
`attributes(ff)` shows you the two attributes that make the difference.

So the class factor is an integer vector with two attributes: levels and class.
Not too important for us right now, but good to keep in mind — it explains a lot
of otherwise surprising behaviour.

## Slide 8 · Factors

Factors are used to represent ordinal or categorical data. Elements of factors
can take one out of several pre-specified values, the levels. And as we just saw,
factors are integers with the attributes levels and class.

We create factors using the function `factor()`, which takes a vector and an
optional argument `levels`.

Two questions to try out. First: what happens if we do not specify levels
explicitly? R derives them from the data and sorts them alphabetically — which is
often not the order you want.

Second, and more consequential: what happens if the vector contains elements not
pre-specified as levels? Those elements silently become NA. That is a classic way
to lose data without noticing, so always check your levels after creating a
factor.

## Slide 9 · Ordered factors and `table()`

Usually levels are not ordered, but for ordinal data you can use the argument
`ordered`. With an ordered factor, comparisons such as greater than become
meaningful.

There are some useful factor-specific functions, such as `table()`. Try it on the
factors you defined so far and work out what it does. The follow-up question is
the instructive one: how do you make sure that the frequency of elements which do
not show up in the vector is still displayed, as zero? That is precisely what the
`levels` argument buys you, and it is why factors exist at all.

One general remark from practice: it is usually better to store categorical data
as character, and only transform them into factors when you actually need the
level machinery — for a plot order, or for a model. Factors that are created too
early are a frequent source of silent NAs.

## Slide 11 · Data frames

Data frames are special lists of vectors where the length of each vector is
equal. That is the whole definition — and it means most list operations also work
for data frames, including the double bracket and the dollar sign from part one.

We usually represent data frames as tables. Each column of the table is one
vector, and the column names are the names of the list elements.

To create a data frame from scratch use `data.frame()`; to create one from an
existing list use `as.data.frame()`.

If you read data into R, it almost always starts off as a data.frame. How to
transform them is the main subject of the sessions on data wrangling later in the
semester.

## Slide 12 · Data frames and tibbles

A modern version of the data.frame is the tibble, from the package of the same
name. We will mostly use tibbles in this course, but do familiarise yourself with
the differences to the data.frame, which continues to be widespread — the tutorial
reading covers this.

To transform a data.frame, or a list, into a tibble, use `tibble::as_tibble()`.

To extract single columns use the single or double bracket operators. And the two
questions should feel familiar from part one: single brackets give you back a
tibble with one column, double brackets give you the underlying vector. Test the
type of a column with `typeof()` after extracting it with double brackets.

## Slide 13 · Getting an overview, and R dialects

To get a quick overview about the content of a data frame, use
`dplyr::glimpse()` or `head()`. A complete overview can be obtained via `View()`,
which opens a spreadsheet-like viewer.

Data frames are among the most widely used data types in R. There are different
approaches to how to handle and transform them, each associated with an R
dialect.

We mainly rely on the tidyverse dialect, which is the easiest to learn and
comprehend, and which is built upon tibbles. The alternatives are the base
dialect, the classical one, and data.table, the fastest one; those mainly use
data.frames and data.tables.

This is genuinely useful to keep in mind when searching for help on the internet:
if an answer on Stack Overflow looks completely alien, it is often not wrong —
it is written in a different dialect.

## Slide 14 · Final exercises

Five final exercises that combine everything from both parts.

For the relative frequencies, combine `table()` with division by the length, or
look at `prop.table()`.

The third exercise is a deliberate trap: the `"char"` column must contain the
numbers six to ten as character, so you need `as.character()` — and afterwards
you should check with `typeof()` that the two columns really have different
types.

The last one is the single-versus-double-bracket distinction one final time.

## Slide 15 · Summary and outlook

This was the last session on the fundamentals of R. We learned about the most
important object types in R, and we saw that functions do different things when
applied to different objects — which is why understanding object types is
absolutely fundamental, and why we spent two sessions on it.

The next session will be dedicated to recap and practising. I will explain
unclear concepts and answer open questions, so use the Moodle forum to tell me
what is unclear, and we will do some exercises together in class.

The usual three tasks until next time.
